body.text: In Labor's Victorian heartland, it's no sure thing Ben Carroll will win his own seat of Niddrie
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll has served as the local member in Niddrie for 14 years but analysts suggest he could make history by losing his own seat in the state election.
The district of Niddrie, which takes in suburbs in Melbourne's north-west including Airport West and Keilor, is Labor heartland, and has been held by the party for its entire 50-year history.
But Labor's margin has been shrinking.
In 2018, Labor's two-party preferred margin was over 12 per cent. At the 2022 election, Mr Carroll won Niddrie on a margin of 6.7 per cent.
On current polls, which suggest Labor could record the worst primary vote of any sitting government in Australia since at least World War II, Mr Carroll is in trouble.
"Ben Carroll is the underdog in that seat," said RedBridge Group pollster Tony Barry, a former Liberal strategist.
Mr Carroll's Liberal challenger is former Moonee Valley councillor Samantha Byrne, who was coy about her chances when asked at a pre-poll earlier this week.
"I'm not taking anything for granted,"
The Liberal campaign faithful were more ambitious when she was introduced as "the next member for Niddrie" at the party's campaign launch last Sunday to rapturous applause.
While Ms Byrne is the most likely alternative member for Niddrie (and strongly favoured by bookmakers), Mr Carroll will face off against nine other local challengers.

That includes One Nation's candidate Jason Taverna, a property investor and business owner who could draw a significant first preference vote, as well as Greens candidate Lana Nguyen, a community arts worker.
If Mr Carroll loses, he would become the first Victorian premier to lose his seat in more than 80 years.
Monash University political historian Paul Strangio said it would make Mr Carroll the first premier to lose a seat in parliament in the "modern era" of Victorian politics.
The last premier to lose their seat in Victoria was Liberal Ian Macfarlan in 1945, but it was in a complicated set of circumstances.
Mr Strangio said that loss belonged to a different political era when the state had a three-party system that created "chaos and revolving door premierships".
Modern pressures on show
When the ABC spoke to voters in Niddrie this week, the cracks in the major party system and pressures endured by a formerly loyal Labor voter base were on show.
Outside a shopping centre in Keilor East, a surprising number of voters were keen to chat politics, and more than one appeared to hold genuine respect for their long-serving local MP.
Dennis Marinakis, 64, described Mr Carroll as "a beautiful man" who had "done some very good things for Niddrie".
The second-generation Greek-Australian has lived in the area for nearly three decades. More than a quarter of Niddrie's residents have southern European ancestry.
Mr Marinakis said he has been a loyal Labor voter most of his life. But he said it was time for change because Labor had lost its "spark".
"We kept voting them in because we were like, 'Oh, traditionally I always voted for Labor', but now people are going, 'I think I might give somebody else a go'," he said.
For him, One Nation was that next option. And while Pauline Hanson, a federal senator, is not on the ballot in next week's Victorian election, the Queenslander had clearly caught Mr Marinakis's eye.
"Liberal proved they can't do anything. Labor's proved they can't do anything.
"Pauline Hanson, give her a go. Why not?"
Some loyal to 'nice guy' Carroll, while others undecided
Another voter described the Mr Carroll as "a nice guy" who had "inherited a hell of a lot of baggage from the last two premiers".
"I'll still be voting for Ben Carroll, but well, I don't know whether my vote will help him too much," he said.
Others were caught up with daily struggles, but weren't yet sure how that would affect their vote.
Niddrie voter Danielle Langdowa said she had been a Labor voter most of her life but was currently undecided.
She said she was desperate for a government that "backs up what they are saying".
"The way food goes up, petrol goes up, everything goes up and we don't have it … that's what's really frustrating," she said.
Mr Barry, the pollster, said there was a "soft edge" to the firming vote in Niddrie that Mr Carroll could potentially win back in the last week of the campaign.
Labor has been making some deals with the electorate already. It has pledged a long-awaited station at Keilor East, now slated to open in 2031, as part of the planned airport rail route.

The station was not recommended by airport rail business case, which in 2022 found "the transport system outcomes [of a station at Keilor East] do not yet provide justification for the additional cost".

The government has spruiked the new station as servicing "around 5,200 passengers daily," a figure that the ABC queried as it would put the new station on par with busy suburban rail hubs like Oakleigh, Sunshine or Craigieburn.
A spokesperson for Victoria's Infrastructure Development Authority clarified this figure referred to transport modelling of "all passengers touching on and off at the station".
The true passenger number may thus be substantially lower.
The promise to prioritise the opening of a Keilor East station before the airport rail project is finished is viewed by some transport experts as a political one.
Still, even that pledge has become politically neutralised since being matched by the Liberals.
For some locals, it was another example of something long been talked about but never done.
Keilor Park voter John, who has lived in the area for 57 years, quipped: "I won't be alive by the time that train comes."
Ms Byrne, the Liberal candidate, said residents of Niddrie felt "Labor have neglected this area for so long".
Labor has also pledged road upgrades, a new pedestrian crossing, and a $200,000 lighting upgrade at a soccer field in Keilor Park.
Yet local promises might not be enough to save the premier.
"These sort of promises aren't shifting the dial," Mr Barry said.
"Most voters are seeing it too little too late."
